integrityMatters.title: Police assessment of altered City of Sydney travel figures cited in Mr Taylor's 2019 letter to the Lord Mayor of Sydney; no further investigation by the Australian Federal Police
integrityMatters.organisation: NSW Police Force (Strike Force Garrad); Australian Federal Police; Commonwealth Ombudsman (review of the AFP's handling)
integrityMatters.description: In September 2019 Mr Taylor, then Minister for Energy and Emissions Reduction, wrote to the Lord Mayor of Sydney citing City of Sydney travel spending figures that did not match the council's published annual report; the figures were reported by The Daily Telegraph. After the Shadow Attorney-General referred the matter to NSW Police, Strike Force Garrad investigated and in December 2019 referred the matter to the Australian Federal Police because the alleged conduct occurred in Canberra. On 6 February 2020 the AFP announced it would not investigate further, stating there was no evidence to indicate the Minister was involved in falsifying information and citing the Minister's apology to the Lord Mayor, the low level of harm and the resources that further investigation would require. The Commonwealth Ombudsman later examined the AFP's handling and found its decision lawful, while noting that the AFP had not tested its resource concerns by seeking further information from the Minister's office. Mr Taylor denied that he or his staff altered the document and apologised for relying on incorrect figures.

statusHistory.note: The Shadow Attorney-General wrote to the NSW Police Commissioner alleging that figures in Mr Taylor's letter of 29 September 2019 to the Lord Mayor were drawn from an altered version of the City of Sydney's annual report. The same day Mr Taylor tabled a statement saying two versions of the report had appeared on the council's website.

NSW Police confirmed that Strike Force Garrad was investigating (date per the Commonwealth Ombudsman's chronology). On 31 October 2019 Mr Taylor wrote to the Lord Mayor acknowledging the figures were incorrect and apologising; on 25 November 2019 he told the House that neither he nor his staff had altered the document.

NSW Police referred the matter to the Australian Federal Police, as the alleged conduct occurred in Canberra, and finalised its own investigation. The AFP confirmed receipt of the referral on 2 January 2020.

The AFP announced it would not investigate further: there was 'no evidence to indicate the Minister for Energy and Emissions Reduction was involved in falsifying information' and further investigation was unlikely to obtain sufficient evidence to substantiate a Commonwealth offence. No charges were laid.

The Commonwealth Ombudsman reported on the AFP's handling of the referral, finding the AFP's decision was 'lawful and open to it' while observing that the AFP had not tested its resource concerns by seeking further information from the Minister's office by less formal means. The report made no finding about Mr Taylor.

integrityMatters.outcome: No charges. Australian Federal Police, 6 February 2020: 'The AFP assessment of this matter identified there is no evidence to indicate the Minister for Energy and Emissions Reduction was involved in falsifying information ... the AFP has determined it is unlikely further investigation will result in obtaining sufficient evidence to substantiate a Commonwealth offence. The AFP now considers this matter finalised.' Commonwealth Ombudsman, 16 November 2020: it was 'lawful and open to it to refrain from further investigating the matter'.

integrityMatters.title: Auditor-General's performance audit of grants under the Supporting Reliable Energy Infrastructure Program, including the Collinsville feasibility-study grant approved by Mr Taylor as Minister
integrityMatters.organisation: Australian National Audit Office (Auditor-General Report No. 31 of 2020-21)
integrityMatters.description: The Auditor-General examined whether the award of two grants under the $10 million Supporting Reliable Energy Infrastructure Program, including $3.61 million to Shine Energy for a feasibility study into a coal-fired power station at Collinsville, Queensland, was informed by an appropriate assessment process and sound advice consistent with the Commonwealth Grants Rules and Guidelines. Mr Taylor, then Minister for Energy and Emissions Reduction, approved the grants on departmental briefings. The report concluded that the award of funding 'was not fully informed by an appropriate assessment process and sound advice' and that aspects of the approach did not comply with the Grants Rules; it found conflict-of-interest and probity arrangements had not been implemented, that the department's advice on the Shine Energy grant was 'partially appropriate' and not consistent with its own assessment that some eligibility requirements and appraisal criteria had not been met, and that the briefings did not clearly identify the extent to which each application met the selection criteria. Its three recommendations were directed to the Department of Industry, Science, Energy and Resources, which agreed to them. The report made no finding of misconduct against the Minister.

statusHistory.note: Report tabled. The ANAO noted that the two funding briefings 'provided a record of the basis for the Minister's decisions to award funding'; its recommendations were directed to the department.

integrityMatters.outcome: ANAO conclusion: 'The award of funding under the Supporting Reliable Energy Infrastructure Program was not fully informed by an appropriate assessment process and sound advice on the award of grant funding. Aspects of the approach did not comply with the Commonwealth Grants Rules and Guidelines.' All three recommendations, directed to the department, were agreed. No finding was made against the Minister personally.

integrityMatters.title: Senate committee majority report on Mr Taylor's 2017 representations about the grasslands listing while a compliance case was open against Jam Land Pty Ltd, a company in which he holds an indirect interest
integrityMatters.organisation: Senate Environment and Communications References Committee; Department of the Environment and Energy (EPBC Act compliance, concerning the company); Federal Court of Australia (concerning the company)
integrityMatters.description: The federal Environment Department investigated the 2016 spraying of critically endangered native grassland on a Monaro property owned by Jam Land Pty Ltd, a company of which Mr Taylor's brother is a director and in which Mr Taylor holds an indirect interest through a family company. In March 2017, while that compliance case was open, Mr Taylor, then Assistant Minister for Cities, sought and attended a meeting with department officials about the listing of the grassland community and raised the listing with the then Environment Minister. This became public in 2019. In December 2019 a majority of the Senate Environment and Communications References Committee (Labor and Greens senators) concluded that his conduct breached the Statement of Ministerial Standards and recommended that the Prime Minister commission a review by the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet; Coalition senators dissented, citing departmental evidence that compliance matters were not discussed at the meeting. No review outcome and no finding by any police, integrity or judicial body about Mr Taylor has been located. Separately, the department issued Jam Land a remediation determination in April 2020, affirmed on reconsideration in December 2021, and the Federal Court dismissed the company's judicial review application in September 2022; Mr Taylor was not a party and is not mentioned in the judgment.

statusHistory.note: Following media reports about the March 2017 meeting, Mr Taylor made a statement to the House of Representatives. The following day a Senate motion to establish a dedicated inquiry was defeated 28 votes to 29.

Interim report of the Senate Environment and Communications References Committee inquiry into Australia's faunal extinction crisis (chapter 3). The Labor and Greens majority concluded Mr Taylor 'consciously used his position as an MP and Minister to make representations to Minister Frydenberg that were aimed at affecting the outcome of the Jam Land compliance case' and that this represented 'clear breaches of the Statement of Ministerial Standards'. Coalition senators dissented: 'The evidence provided by the Department confirms that Mr Taylor has acted appropriately and in accordance with the rules.' Date per reporting of the report's release.

A delegate of the Environment Minister issued Jam Land Pty Ltd a remediation determination under the EPBC Act over the spraying of a 28.5-hectare paddock in October 2016, requiring rehabilitation of 103 hectares of native grassland. This action concerned the company, not Mr Taylor.
The remediation determination was affirmed on ministerial reconsideration.

Jam Land Pty Ltd v Minister for the Environment [2022] FCA 1058: the Federal Court dismissed the company's application for judicial review with costs. Mr Taylor was not a party and is not mentioned in the judgment.

integrityMatters.outcome: Senate committee majority, December 2019: Mr Taylor's conduct 'represents clear breaches of the Statement of Ministerial Standards'; recommended that the Prime Minister ask the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to review the conduct of Mr Taylor and the then Treasurer in relation to the grasslands matter. Coalition senators' dissent: Mr Taylor 'has acted appropriately and in accordance with the rules'. No review by the Prime Minister's department and no finding by any police, integrity or judicial body about Mr Taylor has been located. Concerning the company: the department found Jam Land Pty Ltd breached the EPBC Act and the Federal Court dismissed its judicial review application.

integrityMatters.title: Australian Federal Police investigation into the disclosure to media of the October 2017 searches of Australian Workers' Union offices; no prosecution
integrityMatters.organisation: Australian Federal Police; Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions
integrityMatters.description: On 24 October 2017 the Australian Federal Police, acting for the Registered Organisations Commission, searched Australian Workers' Union offices in Sydney and Melbourne; television crews were in place before officers arrived. At Senate estimates the next day Senator Cash, then Minister for Employment, said several times that her office had not alerted the media, then returned to correct her evidence after her senior media adviser admitted tipping off journalists and resigned. At her request the AFP investigated the disclosure and in mid-2018 provided a brief of evidence to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions. On 15 January 2019 the AFP announced that the CDPP would not prosecute because there were no reasonable prospects of conviction. No charges were laid against anyone. Senator Cash's office said neither she nor her office had been under investigation; at estimates in February 2019 the AFP said it had sought formal witness statements from Senator Cash and Minister Keenan, who declined interviews and provided written statements.

statusHistory.note: Senator Cash corrected her evidence to Senate estimates after her senior media adviser admitted alerting journalists to the searches and resigned.
The AFP confirmed it was investigating the disclosure; Senator Cash had asked for the investigation.
The AFP provided a brief of evidence to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions in July 2018 (exact date not published; reported by the ABC on 15 January 2019).
AFP: 'The CDPP has advised they will not be proceeding with a prosecution as there are no reasonable prospects of conviction.' The AFP considered the investigation complete.

At Senate estimates the AFP said it had wanted formal witness statements from Ministers Cash and Keenan; both declined interviews and provided written statements. The CDPP's representative said there was prima facie evidence that an offence had occurred but no reasonable prospects of conviction.

integrityMatters.outcome: No charges against anyone. Australian Federal Police, 15 January 2019: 'The AFP can confirm the CDPP has advised they will not be proceeding with a prosecution as there are no reasonable prospects of conviction.'

integrityMatters.title: Federal Court findings in the Australian Workers' Union's challenge to the Registered Organisations Commission investigation, including the allegation that it was commenced for an improper political purpose connected to the Minister
integrityMatters.organisation: Federal Court of Australia (Bromberg J; Full Court: Allsop CJ, Besanko and White JJ)
integrityMatters.description: After Senator Cash, as Minister for Employment, referred media reports about Australian Workers' Union donations to GetUp! to the Registered Organisations Commission in August 2017, the Commission opened an investigation that led to the October 2017 searches of AWU offices. The AWU challenged the investigation in the Federal Court, alleging among other things that it had been commenced for an improper political purpose connected to the Minister; Senator Cash and her former staff were subpoenaed and gave evidence. In October 2019 Justice Bromberg found the alleged improper purpose was 'not demonstrated on the evidence', while holding part of the investigation invalid on a statutory-interpretation ground. In November 2020 the Full Court allowed the Commission's appeal on that ground and found that 'the interaction between the Minister and the delegate did not give rise to jurisdictional error'. No adverse finding was made against Senator Cash in either judgment.

statusHistory.note: In its judicial review proceedings against the Commission, the AWU alleged a 'misuse of government powers by Minister Michaelia Cash, to commence an investigation into her perceived political enemies'; Senator Cash and former staff were subpoenaed to give evidence.

Australian Workers' Union v Registered Organisations Commissioner (No 9) [2019] FCA 1671: Bromberg J found the alleged improper purpose was 'not demonstrated on the evidence', while holding one limb of the investigation invalid on a statutory ground.

Registered Organisations Commissioner v Australian Workers' Union [2020] FCAFC 202: the Full Court allowed the Commission's appeal and found 'the interaction between the Minister and the delegate did not give rise to jurisdictional error'.

integrityMatters.outcome: No adverse finding against Senator Cash. First instance: the alleged improper purpose was 'not demonstrated on the evidence'. Full Court: 'the interaction between the Minister and the delegate did not give rise to jurisdictional error'; appeal allowed.

integrityMatters.title: Termination of Mr Hastie's Standby Army Reserve service after he declined a Defence request to remove images of himself in uniform from 2016 election material
integrityMatters.description: During the 2016 federal election campaign, Defence asked Mr Hastie, then the Member for Canning and a member of the Standby Army Reserve, to remove images of himself in uniform from campaign material, citing policy that Australian Defence Force members not engage in political activity in uniform without approval. Mr Hastie declined, saying the image reflected his personal and professional history and that as a former officer he was no longer under military authority. The Army issued a notice of intention to terminate his service for failing to comply with directions and Defence policy, and his reserve service was terminated.

statusHistory.note: Defence stated that the Army had issued Mr Hastie with a notice of intention to terminate his service 'because he had failed to comply with directions and Defence policy', and his service was terminated.

integrityMatters.outcome: Department of Defence statement, as quoted by the ABC on 9 June 2016: 'Defence contacted Mr Hastie, a member of the standby Army Reserve, and requested he remove imagery of himself in uniform from election campaign material. Regrettably, Mr Hastie did not comply with this request. Accordingly, the Army issued Mr Hastie with a notice indicating the intention to terminate his service because he had failed to comply with directions and Defence policy.'

independentSources.title: Andrew Hastie, Canning MP, dumped by Army over use of uniform in campaign material
